headline: Motts Basin Launch, Bay Flats Fluke, and a Bridge Bite Worth Losing Sleep For
subhead: With a lazy groundswell rolling into Rockaway, I kept the kayak in the bay this week — and found fluke, bridge bass, and a few surprises in the flats.
body_markdown:
I put the kayak in at Motts Basin off Cross Bay Boulevard Tuesday morning instead of hauling it out to Fort Tilden, and that decision made the whole trip. There's a low groundswell running along the ocean side right now — nothing scary, 2 to 3 feet at a long 10-second period — but it's enough to turn a peaceful paddle into a workout if you're launching through the inlet surf. The bay side stays flat and glassy most mornings before the sea breeze fills in around ten, so if you're kayak fishing this week, that's your window. Get on the water by six, be back at the ramp before the wind starts pushing whitecaps across the open flats by Ruler's Bar.

The fluke bite inside the bay has been the most consistent thing going. I worked the drop-offs along the edge of the flats south of the JFK runways in 12 to 18 feet, drifting the first two hours of the incoming with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail teased with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp strip. Nothing gigantic — most fish ran 15 to 18 inches, a handful of keepers mixed in — but it was a fish every other drift, which for mid-July in the bay is honest work. A few boats working the deeper hole off Big Egg Marsh reported better size, fish pushing 20 inches, on squid strips fished slow along bottom. If you're marking bait on the sounder — and there's plenty of rainfish and small mullet stacked in those channels right now — slow your drift down and let the bucktail hop instead of drag.

Marine Parkway Bridge is still doing what it does for bass, but you have to fish it on their schedule now, not yours. The daytime bite has gone quiet with the water this warm — I'm talking last two hours of outgoing right around dusk into full dark, working live eels or bunker chunks tight to the pilings on the Rockaway side. A guy I trust who fishes there three nights a week landed two fish over 30 inches last Thursday on eels drifted right through the current seam where the tide rips off the abutment. Daytime, forget it — the fish have slid into the deeper, cooler water under the span and won't commit to anything until the light drops and the current starts working bait past them.

Bluefish showed up stronger than I expected along Breezy Point and the surf just west of the inlet. With that ocean water sitting near 73 degrees and that long-period swell stirring bait up off the bar, we've had a few real toothy blitzes early — six to eight in the morning, gone by nine once the boat traffic picks up. Diamond jigs and Kastmasters worked fast through the wash have been getting hit, along with cut bunker chunked out past the breakers for the bigger ones. Nothing sustained, and I want to be straight about that — these are twenty-minute windows, not all-morning affairs. But if you're willing to be there right at first light with the tide dropping, it's been worth the trip more often than not this week.

Porgies are holding steady off Canarsie Pier and around the Cross Bay Bridge pilings, which is where I sent my nephew with a bucket of sandworms and a high-low rig — he came back with a dozen keepers in about two hours fishing the last of the outgoing. Nothing fancy needed there: small hooks, light sinkers, bottom in 15 to 20 feet, and patience. Weakfish, on the other hand, have been a ghost story this year in the bay — I've heard of exactly one legit fish caught off the Bay side near Motts Basin, and that was on a bucktail meant for fluke. If you're specifically hunting weakfish, I wouldn't build a trip around it right now.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd keep leaning on the bay for the daytime bite and save the bridge and surf for the low-light windows. The swell out front doesn't look like it's laying down much before the weekend, so kayak and small-boat guys should keep favoring the inside launches — Motts Basin, Canarsie Pier ramp, or the Cross Bay side — over fighting through the inlet surf. If that groundswell does back off and the ocean flattens out, I'd make a run out to Breezy at first light and see if those blues hold their pattern; that warm water pushing bait tight to the beach is exactly the kind of setup that turns into a real morning if the timing lines up. Bring both rods either way — this is a week where the bay and the ocean are both worth a look, just not at the same hour.
